# ResQAI code evaluation study guide

Read this alongside your IDE. Each file has a purpose statement and a source-order walkthrough. Line numbers refer to the checked-out code at commit `5206438`. A range covers one statement spread over several lines. Blank lines separate ideas and have no runtime effect. Click a file name in the index to jump to its walkthrough, then use the source link to open the file.

## How the three folders fit together

| Folder | What it owns | How it runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `app/` | Main FastAPI API for authentication, help requests, evidence, alerts, donations, missions, volunteering, the quiz, and AI endpoints | The local Compose service `python-api` runs `app.main:app` on port 8000. |
| `ai-service/` | Standalone FastAPI service for first-aid chat, report translation, summaries, and hospital recommendations | Its own Dockerfile runs `main:app` with a default port of 8001. The checked-in Compose file has no separate service for this folder. |
| `ml-models/` | Training and serving experimental flood-class and risk-score models, with an additional rainfall-based landslide screening rule | The local Compose service runs `api:app` on port 5005. The standalone Dockerfile defaults to 10000 and Compose overrides it. |

The mobile Compose configuration points both the general API and AI API at port 8000. In that setup, `app/routers/ai.py` actually handles requests to `/api/ai`. The standalone service publishes similar URLs with different validation and fallback behavior. For example, the main API AI locator receives a hospital list in its request body. The standalone locator queries PostgreSQL/PostGIS for candidates.

### Three flows to be able to explain aloud

1. **First-aid chat.** A router receives JSON and FastAPI validates it. The chat handler chooses a language and checks the message for high-priority phrases. An immediate response can return before the Gemini call. On ordinary requests, the handler uses an LLM wrapper and maps its outcome to a client response, including a fallback on service failure. The language and urgency heuristics are software rules. The first-aid strings quoted in the walkthrough are application content.
2. **Help request.** The main API resolves the current user or guest, validates the request, derives initial triage from the report, and writes a PostgreSQL record. It separates public and private response fields and records later status changes. Owner checks, coordinator verification, and notification delivery are separate steps. A successful login establishes access under a role. The report still has its own verification status.
3. **Automatic flood assessment.** The ML API validates the district and optional GPS pair. The provider client selects a location and aggregates the last complete Sri Lanka local day plus the needed rainfall history. The prediction engine builds the twelve training features, uses saved encoders, returns a Random Forest class and a separate regressor score, and adds a project threshold-based landslide estimate. The provider data is modeled weather. The evaluation metrics come from a held-out portion of the modeled training CSV and measure performance on that dataset.

### Python concepts you will see repeatedly

| Code | What it means here |
| --- | --- |
| `@router.post(...)` and `include_router(..., prefix=...)` | The decorator sets the HTTP method and local route. The prefix in the entry point determines the full URL. |
| `BaseModel` and `Field(...)` | A Pydantic model defines a data contract. `...` makes a field required. A default supplies an omitted value. An annotation such as `str \| None` allows a JSON null, while a default of `None` also allows omission. |
| `Depends(get_db)` and `Depends(require_role(...))` | FastAPI executes the dependency and injects the resulting session or caller identity. A dependency can reject a request before the handler runs. |
| `async def`, `await`, and `yield` | Async code can give control back to the event loop while waiting. The dependency or lifespan can yield a resource and resume later for cleanup. Synchronous I/O or model inference still needs an executor or thread pool when called from an async handler. |
| `db.add`, `flush`, `commit`, `rollback`, and `refresh` | Add stages an ORM object. Flush issues pending SQL inside the current transaction. Commit persists the transaction. Rollback abandons its uncommitted work. Refresh reads back database state. |
| `HTTPException` | Stops route execution with an intentional HTTP response such as 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429, or 503. Business checks and input-schema validation can reject requests at different stages. |
| `try`, `except`, and `finally` | Code attempts work, handles named failures, and can release resources whether the attempt succeeds or raises. |
| `__name__ == "__main__"` | The block is for direct script execution. Importing the module for an ASGI server or a test skips it. |
| `pytest.fixture`, `monkeypatch`, and `assert` | A fixture supplies setup or input. Monkeypatch temporarily replaces an environment value or dependency. An assertion checks the observable behavior. |

### Start with the open file in your IDE

In [`ai-service/models/schemas.py`](../ai-service/models/schemas.py), the request classes describe incoming JSON and the response classes describe outgoing JSON. There is no database access or Gemini call in this file. For example, `FirstAidRequest` requires a nonempty message of up to 2,000 characters and defaults the language to `auto`. A valid body reaches the chatbot. Its output is described by `FirstAidResponse`, where the renderer can use `is_critical`, `show_1990`, and `service_available` independently. In [`app/__init__.py`](../app/__init__.py), the package marker lets the main API be imported through the `app` namespace used by `app.main:app`.

Try tracing two request bodies before reading the implementation:

| JSON body sent to the standalone chat route | What the schema does |
| --- | --- |
| `{"message":"hello"}` | Accepts the string and fills in `language="auto"`. The router then chooses a language and follows its chat flow. |
| `{"message":""}` | Rejects the empty string at the minimum-length check. FastAPI returns a validation response before the router calls Gemini. |

### Questions you may get in an evaluation

- **Why have separate Pydantic and ORM models?** Pydantic validates the HTTP contract. SQLAlchemy maps durable rows and relationships. A route can expose a purpose-built response without returning every database column.
- **Why use PostgreSQL and Redis?** PostgreSQL holds persistent records and provides PostGIS spatial operations. Redis holds short-lived authentication state, counters, cooldowns, and evidence challenges.
- **What is the difference between authentication and authorization?** Authentication derives a caller from a bearer token and stored account/session state. Authorization checks roles, ownership, and sometimes a more specific workflow requirement.
- **Why keep the encoders with the trained models?** The same district and climate labels must map to the same numeric features at training and inference time. A different fitted encoder can change what a number means.
- **Why do the classifier and regressor both exist?** The classifier predicts one category and exposes class probabilities. The regressor predicts a numeric score. The project separately applies thresholds to the landslide profile and 24-hour rain.
- **Why distinguish missing weather from zero rain?** Zero rain can be a real, valid sample. Missing or invalid hours make the automatic feature vector incomplete, so the route returns a weather-unavailable response before inference.
- **Why are there two time windows in weather aggregation?** Rain values are preceding-hour amounts and include the midnight endpoint. State values represent instantaneous samples and use the preceding day's midnight through its last hour.
- **What do the recorded ML metrics establish?** Accuracy is the fraction of correct class predictions on the test split, MAE is the mean absolute score error, and R² measures fit relative to the test target mean. These are results on modeled data from a random split. Independent observed-event validation would be needed to establish field performance.
- **Why have a deterministic fallback?** Database lookups and simple rules can produce useful structured output when an upstream AI request fails. Emergency warnings can appear before waiting on an LLM.
- **What does startup verify?** The main API checks its signing-key configuration, PostgreSQL/schema compatibility, and Redis. The standalone AI service logs degraded database availability and can start. The ML API checks artifacts on demand.

### `ai-service/.env.example`

Documents placeholder configuration for the Gemini models, deadlines, database, and server.

### `ai-service/routers/locator.py`

Retrieves three nearby hospital candidates through PostGIS and asks Gemini for a recommendation among those available.

<a id="ml-models-dockerfile"></a>

### `ml-models/Dockerfile`

Installs prediction dependencies and serves the ML API in its own container.

[Open source](../ml-models/Dockerfile)

- **[L2](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L2)** `FROM python:3.11-slim` — Uses the indicated base image as the starting filesystem and runtime.
- **[L4](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L4)** `WORKDIR /app` — Sets the default directory for subsequent build instructions and the container process.
- **[L6](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L6)** `ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` — Sets an environment variable available to subsequent instructions and the process.
- **[L7](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L7)** `ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` — Sets an environment variable available to subsequent instructions and the process.
- **[L8](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L8)** `ENV PORT=10000` — Sets an environment variable available to subsequent instructions and the process.
- **[L10](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L10)** `COPY requirements.txt .` — Copies the indicated build-context files into the image.
- **[L12](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L12)** `RUN pip install --no-cache-dir \` — Runs the build-time command in the image layer.
- **[L13](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L13)** `--default-timeout=1000 \` — Continues the preceding build instruction.
- **[L14](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L14)** `--retries 10 \` — Continues the preceding build instruction.
- **[L15](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L15)** `-r requirements.txt` — Continues the preceding build instruction.
- **[L17](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L17)** `COPY . .` — Copies the indicated build-context files into the image.
- **[L19](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L19)** `EXPOSE 10000` — Documents the container's listening port. Compose or the runtime publishes ports explicitly.
- **[L21](../ml-models/Dockerfile#L21)** `CMD ["sh", "-c", "exec uvicorn api:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port ${PORT:-10000}"]` — Defines the default command when the built container starts.

### `ml-models/datasets/sri_lanka_districts.csv`


[Open source](../ml-models/datasets/sri_lanka_districts.csv)

Line 1 defines 7 columns. The next 25 records are data.

- `district` — Sri Lankan district identifier used for category encoding and lookup.
- `province` — Administrative province associated with the district.
- `zone` — District climate description consumed at inference.
- `primary_river_basin` — River basin attached to the district profile.
- `landslide_prone_zone` — District-level profile used by the rainfall screening.
- `elevation_category` — General district elevation description.
- `major_hazard_profile` — Other hazards represented by the district profile.

<a id="ml-models-datasets-sri-lanka-flood-risk-modeled-csv"></a>

### `ml-models/datasets/sri_lanka_flood_risk_modeled.csv`


[Open source](../ml-models/datasets/sri_lanka_flood_risk_modeled.csv)

Line 1 defines 19 columns. The next 91,325 records are data.

- `date` — Date of the modeled record.
- `precipitation_sum` — Daily total precipitation used as an input feature.
- `rain_sum` — Daily rainfall total used as an input feature.
- `soil_moisture_0_to_7cm_mean` — Average shallow soil moisture.
- `soil_moisture_7_to_28cm_mean` — Average deeper soil moisture.
- `temperature_2m_max` — Daily maximum temperature at two metres.
- `wind_speed_10m_max` — Daily maximum wind speed at ten metres.
- `district` — Sri Lankan district identifier used for category encoding and lookup.
- `latitude` — Latitude stored for the modeled record.
- `longitude` — Longitude stored for the modeled record.
- `province` — Administrative province associated with the district.
- `climatic_zone` — Training climate category for encoding.
- `rain_24h` — Twenty-four-hour accumulated rainfall feature.
- `rain_48h` — Forty-eight-hour accumulated rainfall feature.
- `rain_72h` — Seventy-two-hour accumulated rainfall feature.
- `soil_saturation_index` — Combined soil-moisture feature.
- `year` — Calendar year stored for the modeled record.
- `flood_risk_score` — Regression training target.
- `flood_category` — Classification training target.

The first data row is an Ampara example dated 2015-01-01. Training builds its feature matrix from selected fields plus encoded district and climate columns. The date, year, coordinates, and province are retained dataset context and are outside that feature matrix.
